subject: Meteorology
title: The Low-Level Jet
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Low-Level Jet.

hook.text: After sunset, a ribbon of fast-moving air often develops around 1 km altitude—the low-level jet (LLJ).

buildup.text: As surface friction drops at night, winds above the boundary layer accelerate—sometimes reaching 50 knots or more.

discovery.text: The LLJ transports warm, moist Gulf air northward into the Great Plains—feeding overnight thunderstorms.

twist.text: The LLJ also increases wind shear, helping storms organize into squall lines and MCSs after dark.

climax.text: Many of the worst flash floods in US history occurred from nocturnal MCSs fueled by the low-level jet.

punchline.text: Nighttime brings a hidden wind—and it fuels storms you can't see.

quiz.question: What fuels the low-level jet at night?
